# Start here {#quickstart}

Use this chapter if you are about to submit a paper and need to get the code
behind it ready to share. It covers the minimum steps to turn your project
folder into an archive that someone else can download, open and run.

::: {.tada-key}
Work through the project roughly in this order: fix the **paths and file
types**, **annotate** the scripts (ideally you have been annotating as you go;
see [Annotated](#annotated-asyougo)), write the **README**, and ask a colleague
to run the whole thing. Then **archive** it and get a DOI. Archiving last means the
DOI points to the version that has already been checked.
:::

::: {.tada-wiki}
The checklist below is grouped by TADA principle, not by the order you do the
work. Run the project from a clean copy of your folder first, then archive it,
then run it once more from the archived download. If that second run breaks, fix
the problem and publish a new version of the deposit, and cite the final
version.
:::

Just want the tick list? [Jump to the checklist](#quickstart-checklist).

## The pre-submission checklist {#quickstart-checklist}

:::: {.tada-checklist-head}
::: {.tada-dog-float}
![](assets/figures/dog-sad.png){.tada-dog-sad alt="A sad cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
![](assets/figures/dog-happy.png){.tada-dog-happy alt="A happy cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
:::

::: {.tada-dog-hint}
Try doing all of these to make the dog happy.
:::
::::

TADA covers your code. The data have their own short list. Tick every box and see what happens.

::: {.tabset}

### Code (TADA) {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Condensed from the TADA guidelines.

**Transferable** — [full chapter](#transferable)

- [ ] Every script is saved with a standard code extension (`.R`, `.py`, `.cpp`, …), not inside a `.docx` or `.pdf`
- [ ] No `setwd()` (R) or `os.chdir()` (Python) appears anywhere in the code
- [ ] No absolute paths (`/Users/you/…`, `C:/Users/you/…`) remain; paths are [relative](#transferable-paths) (written from the project folder, e.g. `data/raw/file.csv`)
- [ ] Data, code and materials all live in **one** project directory
- [ ] The project runs successfully from a clean start (restart R or Python with nothing already loaded: in RStudio use *Session → Restart R* and clear the Environment pane with the broom icon; in Jupyter, restart the kernel)

**Available** — [full chapter](#available)

- [ ] Code is deposited in an [immutable repository](#available-where) (files can't be changed after publishing) that gives it a persistent identifier such as a DOI (Zenodo, Figshare, …)
- [ ] The DOI is **[cited in the manuscript text and reference list](#available-cite)**
- [ ] If the code was developed on GitHub, a release (a fixed, labelled snapshot of the code) has been created and linked to Zenodo or Figshare, since [GitHub is not an archive](#available-github) and does not produce DOIs

**Documented** — [full chapter](#documented)

- [ ] A [`README.md`](#documented-readme) (or `README.txt`) sits at the top of the project
- [ ] It names the manuscript, the authors, a contact address, and any funders
- [ ] It lists software **and version** (e.g. R v4.5.2) and key packages **and versions** (e.g. ggplot2 v4.0.2)
- [ ] It states the licence
- [ ] It says where the data are, ideally with their own DOI
- [ ] It says what each file is, what order to run things in, what the code needs and what it produces
- [ ] It flags anything slow or resource-hungry
- [ ] It says whether and how large language models were used in code generation (SORTEE; not a TADA requirement)
- [ ] A [licence](#documented-licence) is actually attached to the deposit

**Annotated** — [full chapter](#annotated)

- [ ] Code is broken into labelled chunks (blocks of code that do one job, each with a heading comment)
- [ ] Each chunk says *what* it does, *why*, and *which* result it produces ([examples](#annotated-chunks))
- [ ] Signposts point at the manuscript ("produces Figure 3B", "Table 2, column 4")

**Before you submit** — [full chapter](#code-review)

- [ ] Someone else (a colleague or co-author) has run the whole project from the archived files, successfully (if you work alone, see the tip under [A project layout that works](#quickstart-layout))
- [ ] `set.seed()` / `random.seed()` is set before anything that uses random numbers, such as simulations or MCMC (Markov chain Monte Carlo, a method for fitting models by random sampling; [SORTEE Stage 6](#sortee), [Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}; not a TADA requirement; see [Code review](#code-review))

### Data {.unlisted .unnumbered}

::: {.tada-wiki}
This is the data counterpart to the code checklist, condensed from the
[SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) and the [Data & code sharing](#data-sharing)
chapter, where every point is explained in full.
:::

**Archived & citable** — [Available](#available)

- [ ] Data deposited in an [immutable repository](#available-where) with a DOI, cited in the manuscript text and reference list
- [ ] Nothing lives only in supplementary material

**Present & complete** — [what to share](#sharing-what)

- [ ] Raw data archived — or a sample plus the processed data, or a documented route to obtaining them
- [ ] Processed and filtered data archived, or the code that produces them

**Interoperable format** — [file formats](#sharing-formats)

- [ ] Data in `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt` or `.parquet`, not `.xls`, `.sav` or `.pdf`

**Documented** — [metadata](#sharing-metadata)

- [ ] A data README or dictionary describes every file and every variable, **with units**
- [ ] Collection date and location, funders, and any derived-data sources are recorded

**Licensed** — [data licences](#sharing-licences)

- [ ] A data licence is chosen and stated (CC0 or CC BY are the usual choices)

:::

::: {.tada-wiki}
The most useful check on this page is to **download your own archived deposit
into a fresh, empty folder, ideally on a different machine, and run it.** It catches the failures the SORTEE guidelines group under
[Stage 5](#sortee): wrong paths, missing packages and missing files ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}). It
will not catch [Stage 6](#sortee) failures, such as stochasticity and version sensitivity.
Those need a seed and a documented environment.
:::

## A project layout that works {#quickstart-layout}

The two conventions in the tree below come from
[Ivimey-Cook et al. (2023, §3.1)]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}.

::: {.tada-wiki}
The layout itself is our own suggestion. The exact layout matters less than whether
a reader can see the order and purpose of every file without asking you.
:::

```
my-project/
├── README.md                 <- start here: what this is, how to run it
├── LICENSE                   <- how others may use the code
├── my-project.Rproj          <- or a Python virtual environment
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                  <- never edited by any script
│   │   └── caterpillars_2024.csv
│   └── processed/            <- written by 01_, read by 02_
│       └── caterpillars_clean.csv
├── R/                        <- or scripts/, or src/
│   ├── 01_clean_data.R
│   ├── 02_fit_models.R
│   └── 03_make_figures.R
├── functions/                <- helpers sourced by the scripts above
│   └── utils.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    └── models/               <- saved model objects for slow fits
```

Two conventions do most of the work.

1. **Numbered scripts.** A reader knows the order to run things in without
   being told: `01_`, `02_`, `03_`.
2. **`data/raw/` is read-only.** Cleaning writes to `data/processed/`. Raw data
   are never modified or overwritten by a script, so a botched cleaning step
   cannot destroy the original.

## Three common causes of failure {#quickstart-mistakes}

The first two rows come from the TADA guidelines and the third from the
SORTEE guidelines ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}, Stage 6).

| Mistake | Why it breaks | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `setwd("C:/Users/ed/Desktop/analysis")` | The path exists on exactly one computer | Open the project through its `.Rproj` file, or start Python inside the project folder, and build paths with `here()` / `pyprojroot` (packages you install; see [Transferable](#transferable-paths)) |
| Code shared as a `.pdf` or `.docx` | Copying and pasting code can change characters such as apostrophes, alter white space, or add line numbers and headers, causing errors that are hard to spot | Save as `.R` / `.py`; see [Transferable](#transferable-filetype) |
| No `set.seed()` before a simulation or MCMC run | Results change every run, so nobody can tell a real mismatch from noise | Set a seed at the top of each independently runnable section; see the example in [The SORTEE guidelines](#sortee-common-failures) |

## The README {#quickstart-readme}

Copy [`templates/README-template.md`](templates/README-template.md) into your
project and replace the angle-bracketed parts. The
[Documented](#documented-readme) chapter explains each field and why it is
there.

Or generate one with [READMEBuilder](https://github.com/EIvimeyCook/READMEBuilder) (`pak::pak("EIvimeyCook/READMEBuilder")`, then `build_readme()`), a Shiny app that fills in these fields from your project and writes the `README.md`.

## Archiving on Zenodo, step by step {#quickstart-zenodo}

::: {.tada-wiki}
Zenodo is free and a sensible default if you are unsure where to deposit
(see [Available](#available-where) for the alternatives). Button names change
occasionally, so check [Zenodo's help](https://help.zenodo.org/) if something
looks different.

1. Make a free account at <https://zenodo.org>. You can log in with ORCID or GitHub.
2. Choose **New upload** and add the files from your project folder (or a single `.zip` of the folder if there are many).
3. Fill in the details: the upload type (**Software** for code), a title, the authors, a description, and a **licence**.
4. Choose **Publish**. Treat the files as permanent from this point. To fix a mistake in the files, create a **New version**, which gets its own DOI.
5. Copy the DOI from the record page. Zenodo gives you two: a version-specific DOI for exactly this upload, and a base DOI that always points to the latest version. See [Available](#available-cite) for which to cite.
:::

## What happens next {#quickstart-next}

::: {.tada-dog-float .tada-dog-float--standalone .is-happy}
![](assets/figures/dog-happy.png){.tada-dog-happy alt="A happy cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
:::


If your target journal has a **data editor**, someone will check your deposit
against criteria similar to those in the [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee)
([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}).
The guidelines set out six stages, ranging from whether the code is archived
under a licence to whether the results reproduce. Read that chapter to
understand what will be checked when your submission is assessed.

If your journal has no data editor, the checks still matter. They fall to you
and your co-authors, through [code review](#code-review).
